note.en: What you see: At the lower PLAPS point on the posterolateral chest, the probe looks at the costophrenic recess where pleural fluid gathers first. In health the diaphragm curves brightly with lung above and liver or spleen below, and the recess angle is sharp. With effusion a dark pocket opens above the diaphragm and the lung floats within it. Consolidation below the line shows liver like tissue with bright air echoes instead of clean aeration.

Common mistakes and correction: Calling the stomach bubble pleural fluid: fluid sits above the diaphragm, stomach below it. Missing a small pocket by sitting too anterior: slide back to the posterolateral line. Mistaking consolidated lung for liver: consolidation holds bright air echoes and moves with breath.

Normal values with units: No numeric threshold applies. In health the recess angle is sharp with no dark pocket above the diaphragm. Any new anechoic pocket in the recess with a breathless patient needs senior review and correlation with the clinical picture.

Pitfalls: Small effusions hide in the angle and appear only in one breath phase, so watch full cycles. In pneumonia the PLAPS point often shows consolidation rather than pure fluid, so record tissue pattern as well as fluid. Mark the pocket position for any planned drainage rather than relying on memory.

todo.en: How to get it step by step: Place the probe at the lower posterolateral BLUE point with the marker toward the head. Find the diaphragm as the bright curve and the recess angle above it. Watch a full breath: fluid appears as a dark pocket that changes with respiration. Sweep up and down to size the pocket and check the lung pattern above it. Repeat on the opposite side for comparison.

q.en: Where does pleural fluid gather first?

o.en: Below the diaphragm with the stomach
Above the diaphragm in the costophrenic recess

why.en: The dependent costophrenic recess above the diaphragm collects fluid first.

q.en: How is pleural fluid separated from stomach bubble?

o.en: Fluid sits above the diaphragm while stomach sits below it

why.en: The diaphragm divides them: fluid above, stomach below.

q.en: A tiny pocket flashes in one breath phase only. What next?

o.en: Watch full breath cycles and compare sides

why.en: Small effusions hide across the cycle, so watch full breaths and compare sides.
